body.text: The ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Telangana (excluding Hyderabad) has resulted in more than 53 lakh electors being placed on the absent, shifted, dead and duplicate (ASDD) list after the enumeration phase. A preliminary analysis by the Sabar Institute suggests that the deletions have a distinct pattern in constituencies won by the BJP in the 2023 Assembly election.

The BJP is “the only party whose 2023 vote share rises with the Muslim share of deletions”, according to Sabar Institute’s analysis. The institute shared with Frontline an exclusive, Statewide preliminary analysis of ASDD data covering 104 Assembly constituencies outside Hyderabad. Telangana has recorded the highest number of draft-roll deletions among the States undergoing the SIR so far, according to Election Commission of India (ECI) data.

In the seven constituencies won by the BJP in 2023, Sabar Institute estimates that in the ASDD list, nearly 45 per cent of the electors marked “untraceable” and 17 per cent of those marked dead are Muslims. In these seven constituencies, the number of Muslim voters marked untraceable is 2.6 times the proportion of Muslim voters marked dead.

The ratio is different in constituencies won by the Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS). There, the number of Muslim voters marked untraceable is 1.2 times the number marked dead, Sabir Ahamed, lead researcher at Sabar Institute, told Frontline. Ashin Chakraborty and Souptik Halder are co-researchers.

Sabar Institute is a crowd-funded research organisation based in Kolkata that works on public policy and evidence-based research, with a focus on disadvantaged communities. It has previously published preliminary analyses of SIR data from Delhi, Hyderabad, Meghalaya, Manipur, Jharkhand (partly), Uttarakhand and West Bengal.

Telangana has 119 Assembly constituencies. Sabar Institute published a separate preliminary analysis of the ASDD data from the 15 Assembly constituencies in Hyderabad in early September. The analysis shared with Frontline covers the remaining 104 constituencies.

In Telangana, the exercise began with the enumeration of existing electors, followed by the publication of a draft roll. Electors whose names were categorised as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate were placed on the ASDD list and left out of the draft roll.
Patterns in ASDD data

The Sabar Institute team analysed the ASDD data to detect patterns of disproportionate impact by constituency, polling station, gender, recorded reasons, geography, and other relevant factors. The immediate focus has been on ASDD deletions, but a report on deletions because of logical discrepancies is in the works, said Sabir.

Telangana had 3.38 crore (precisely 3,38,26,448) electors when the SIR exercise began in the State on June 25. After the enumeration phase, 21.7 per cent of electors were removed from the draft electoral rolls to the ASDD list: 16.99 per cent absent or shifted; 2.73 per cent dead; and 1.98 per cent “duplicate”. Nearly 93 lakh (92,87,577) voters in Telangana received notices for logical discrepancies or for being unmapped with the 2002 special revision list.

In India, the electoral rolls do not contain a religion column. Sabar Institute’s analysis relies on parsing the large data sets from the Election Commission to identify Muslim names. Sabar Institute’s methodology used both string-matching and language-based cross-verification. A voter was counted as bearing a Muslim name only when both the Telugu spelling and the English (Romanised) spelling (in the electoral rolls) bore out the conclusion. If only one of the two spellings was in agreement, the voter was marked as “uncertain”.

While a constituency-wise analysis for the entire State is yet to be published, the organisation shared a booth-level analysis spanning 202 booths where over 90 per cent of the names on the deletions list were Muslim. Nearly 87 per cent of these 202 booths were concentrated in 3 constituencies: Rajendranagar (73), Nizamabad Urban (64), and Maheshwaram (38). In 122 of these 202 booths, the predominant reason given for the deletions was that the voter was untraceable.

“A booth having mostly Muslim deletions is partly a reflection of who lives on that street. The more important question here is why such a large percentage were deemed ‘untraceable’ in one exercise. That can only be answered by ground-verification of those addresses,” Sabir told Frontline.

The report shared with Frontline shows that nearly 1 in 4 Telangana (excluding Hyderabad) electors who voted in the 2023 Assembly election were categorised as ASDD. Nearly 85.8 per cent of the deletions (46.31 lakh people) are marked as shifted, untraceable, or already enrolled elsewhere.
Across Telangana (excluding Hyderabad), Muslim names form 12.5 per cent of all deletions in districts where, according to the 2011 Census, Muslims form 8.8 per cent of the population.

Along with the revision of electoral rolls, a rationalising of polling booths was undertaken by the Election Commission in Telangana. To improve accessibility for voters, booths that had over 1,200 voters underwent rationalisation.
In Sabar’s booth-level analysis, the ASDD data showed that 19 booths in Telangana had over 1,000 voters in the deletion list and over 2,196 booths had at least 500 voters in the deletion list.

Sabar analysed data from 532 booths in Telangana (excluding Hyderabad) to understand the reasons given for deletions. In 512 booths, over 95 per cent of the votes in the deletions list had the same reason: “permanently shifted”. Sabir said: “In 13 of those booths, every single deletion carries the same reason—not one death, not one duplicate entry.”
Women feature prominently in deletions

Analysis of State-wide data (excluding Hyderabad) also showed that around 50.2 per cent of the names on the deletions list are of women. In 91 out of the 104 seats outside Hyderabad, Sabar found that more women than men featured on the deletions list. About 71 per cent of the “deleted” women voters were married and, on average, aged around 45 years. Nearly half of the transgender voters in these 104 seats had their names deleted. In the 2023 electoral rolls, Telangana had 2,350 transgender voters; the names of 1,152 such voters were deleted from the draft rolls after the enumeration phase.

Sabar collected the Election Commission’s own booth-wise deletion lists and compiled them into a spreadsheet. Speaking about the accuracy of Sabar’s methodology, Sabir Ahamed said: “The ECI’s own summary gives the deletion data as total deletion numbers for each district. Our totals for each district matched it exactly in 31 of 32 districts.” In total, Sabar analysed 53,96,806 deleted names against the ECI’s 53,97,791, missing the analysis for only 985 out of nearly 54 lakh deletions from across the state (barring Hyderabad).

Responding to questions about the overall scale of ASDD deletions, Telangana’s Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Sudharsan Reddy, told Frontline: “In congested urban pockets like Hyderabad and its surroundings, it has been a challenge. That is why the numbers have been huge.”

After the publication of the draft electoral rolls, voters pushed to the ASDD list have the option of submitting Form 6, which is the form for registration of new voters, along with the prescribed declaration form. The deadline for submission is October 7; hearings and disposals are under way. There are also provisions for appeal against the decision before the district magistrate or appellate authority. Voters can also appeal to the CEO.
If a voter in the ASDD list cannot find resolution during the period of claims and objections, their name would not feature in the final electoral rolls, scheduled for release on November 9.

Civil society organisations and activists have raised concerns about the accuracy of the deletions and the SIR exercise in Telangana. The onus seems to be on the people to ensure they feature on the final rolls. Meanwhile, the CEO has asked the District Election Officers (DEO) and Electoral Registration Officers (ERO) to carefully verify the ASDD list, particularly the cases where electors had submitted enumeration forms but their names did not appear in the draft electoral roll.

On August 21, two Telangana-based NGOs, ASEEM and ADALAH, wrote to the CEO saying: “If an elector who has been continuously enrolled in previous electoral rolls has now been categorised as Absent, Shifted, Dead, Duplicate or otherwise placed in the ASDD list and his/her name has consequently not appeared in the Draft Electoral Roll, the elector should not be required to approach the system as though he/she is a new elector seeking first-time enrolment.”

On August 29, Chief Minister Revanth Reddy wrote to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar seeking a four-week extension of the claims and objections window. “I would request that this period be extended by four weeks, so that electors whose names are missing from the draft rolls—the ASDD (absent, shifted, dead, duplicate) class particularly—have sufficient time to find out where they stand and to file Form 6 claims,” Reddy wrote. The deadline was subsequently moved from September 16 to October 7 by the ECI.

In the report published in early September about the Hyderabad (15 Assembly constituencies) ASDD list, Sabar found that 40.7 per cent of the names on the list were Muslim. The percentage is not uniform across constituencies: the figure is 12.1 per cent in Secunderabad Cantonment; 85.9 per cent in Bahadurpura.

The most common reason (in 69.3 per cent of the cases) for being dropped from the draft roll was “permanently shifted”. The share of “untraceable” voters on ASDD lists seemed to have a proportionate link with the number of Muslim voters: across all 15 Assembly constituencies of Hyderabad, seats with a higher proportion of Muslim voters seemed to have a higher proportion of deletions marked “untraceable” instead of dead, shifted, or duplicate. Sabar does not claim the analysis has 100 per cent accuracy, but rather that its figures should be read as upper-bounds.

A figure that earlier raised alarm about the scale of deletions in Telangana was that, in two Hyderabad constituencies, Malakpet and Yakutpura, Sabar found that the number of deletions exceeded the number of votes polled in the 2023 Assembly election. Overall, in the 15 constituencies of Hyderabad, the number of deletions added up to 89 per cent of the total votes polled in the 2023 Assembly elections.

“We cannot say that a voter’s deletion was caused by their religion, gender, or other demographic indicator. We can only say that the deletions are significantly correlated or associated with the relevant demographic indicator,” Sabir told Frontline, maintaining that the institute is not attempting a causal analysis.
